articles.title: Jepsen: ParticleDB 1.1.4
articles.content: Background Modern applications often spread state across a variety of systems: databases, caches, queues, data warehouses, search indices, and so on. Coordinating these systems is challenging: caches are often stale, the analytics platform might lag days behind the primary database, the search index might lose data, and transactional updates across disparate systems remains an open research problem . ParticleDB aims to unify these workloads in a single engine with a special focus on AI agents and applications. It offers transactional SQL, a key-value store, vector search, live analytics, and user-defined functions called Particles . To integrate with existing systems, clients can connect through a variety of interfaces , including the Postgres and Redis protocols, as well as its own gRPC and HTTP2 APIs. Written from the ground up in Rust, ParticleDB claims to be orders of magnitude faster than Postgres while preserving the same safety characteristics. ParticleDB was built by Orkes to support their workflow orchestration platform, Conductor . Conductor was initially built to store data in Redis and Postgres, but to improve performance, Orkes opted to write their own database. ParticleDB 1.0.0 offered a limited feature set specifically for Conductor’s queries, and was deployed as the backing database for some of their Conductor clusters. A few Orkes customers followed suit. In preparation for a broader release, Orkes undertook a major refactoring of ParticleDB, adding a custom wire protocol, more datatypes, additional OLAP queries, and more. While Orkes and their customers continued to run 1.0.0, they soft launched the refactored versions on particledb.ai . Orkes engaged Jepsen to test these versions of ParticleDB, beginning with 1.1.4. While ParticleDB could run as a single node, it also offered a replicated cluster using the Raft consensus protocol. This replication feature was available only in enterprise cloud deployments. The builds Orkes provided did not support replication, so this report covers only single-node behavior. Safety ParticleDB’s home page advertised that ParticleDB was “formally proven” with a TLA+ proof. However, during our collaboration no TLA+ specification was available. It is unclear what properties might be proven, or whether they described ParticleDB as built. ParticleDB offered three tactics for syncing its Write-Ahead Log (WAL). The sync mode called fsync on each commit, groupsync batched multiple transactions into a single fsync , and nosync skipped fsync altogether. The Transaction Engine documentation described sync as offering “stronger durability” than groupsync . On the other hand, particledb start --help said the groupsync mode ensured that “COMMIT waits for flush”, and Orkes’ internal operator guide concurred: groupsync offered the “same durability as sync ”. ParticleDB’s home page proudly claimed “Full ACID. 159K TPS.” However, the text immediately below this said “snapshot isolation”, which is not fully isolat
articles.summary: Jepsen 发布 ParticleDB 1.1.4 测试报告，分析多系统状态协调中的缓存过期与索引滞后问题。

articles.title: Simple circuits can create complex behaviors
articles.content: The world is full of surprising behavior: Beavers building dams, songbirds singing, spiders building webs, and you reading this article. All of these behaviors are orchestrated by neurons firing in the brain. But how exactly do collections of neurons create these complex behaviors? This is a huge question that researchers are still working on. But over the last half century, neuroscientists have solved some pieces of this puzzle. In this article, we’ll build a tiny creature called a spark, and we’ll give it a very simple brain. As you’ll see, even this tiny brain can create rich and unexpected behaviors. Light eaters Suppose this spark feeds on light. Its goal in life is to reach the light. The light-hungry spark needs a way to sense the world. So we’ll give it a rudimentary eye — a single neuron that detects brightness and converts it into electrical pulses. It also needs a way to move. So we’ll give it another neuron that can wiggle a flipper. By wiring the first sensory neuron to the second motor neuron , we’ve just assembled our first neural circuit: The anatomy of a spark With this simple circuit, the spark wiggles its flipper in proportion to the amount of light. Can it find the light? If the sparks happen to face the light, they’re drawn towards it. But most of the time, they miss. Over time, their paths look like this: Only a few paths cross the light. Clearly, we can do a lot better… Adding an eye Here’s the problem: While the spark can speed up, it can’t steer. With one eye and one flipper, it only moves in one direction. But we need it to turn. What if we give it another eye and flipper? With two eyes, the spark can now sense whether the light is to its left or right. Now, it moves like this: Hmm… that didn’t work. Instead of steering towards the light, it steered away from it! If you didn’t know how their brains work, you might think that they fear light. Why do they avoid the light? Well, if the light were to the spark’s left, then its left eye would sense more brightness, which means that its left flipper would wiggle faster, and this would cause it to turn right, away from the light. Conversely, if the light were to its right, then it would veer left. A crossed connection But there’s a clever way to make this spark steer towards the light instead. All we have to do is cross its connections. That is, we wire its left eye to its right flipper, and its right eye to its left flipper. With this simple wiring change, it can finally steer towards the light. But if you watch these sparks for a while, you’ll notice that there’s a problem. While they can reach the light, they don’t slow down near it. Instead, they charge towards it like comets plunging towards the sun. If you didn’t know how their brains work, now you might think that they’re attacking the light. Becoming inhibited Why do they attack the light? The problem lies in the type of connection that we used. To see why, we need to go back to our original spark. Remember how its flip

articles.title: HackerTube: YouTube built from videos recommended by HN
articles.content: HackerTube 31 Oct, 2026 It was Friday night at 11pm, I was tired, I went to YouTube to watch something and realized that I was looking at an enshittified wall of slop. Insanely exaggerated thumbnails, dumb recommendations of the same tired topics, truly terrible idiocracy-grade content. I'm sure this algorithm works well for the median person on the internet, but it definitely does not work for me. So this morning (Saturday) I took a hold of my Opus 5.5 and gave it the task: Let's write our own YouTube clone based on whatever videos have been recommended on Hacker News. And Opus came back with: hackertube.org ! Opus downloaded all comments of HackerNews, filtered them down, ran Sonnet over them in a workflow, got rid of spam and low grade content, and narrowed them down to just 40K comments recommending a YouTube video. In total, we get 6,454 YouTube videos that have been recommended by a few people on HN from 2007-2026 across 150 topics. Then we wrap it up in a YouTube UI, get a domain, push to a VPS, secure, harden, optimize and voila! HackerTube: Contains quality content Uses the 50% thumbnail instead of the uploaded thumbnail Custom and good ForYou recommendations without any user accounts, storing state in local browser session Keyboard shortcuts Export of the site's data available to give to your agent to easily create your own version This takes ~2 hours now. I can breathe again. Thank you Opus 5.5 <3.
articles.summary: 开发者因不满 YouTube 推荐质量，用 HN 推荐视频搭建 HackerTube，提供更优质的内容发现方式。

articles.title: An Italian farmer found some unknown seeds in his attic and planted them
articles.content: An Italian Farmer Found Some Unknown Seeds in His Attic and, With Nothing to Lose, Planted Them. The Result Was Almost Biblical When a seven-eared stem emerged from the ground, it seemed like a miracle. What Claudio Grossi had unearthed was an ancient grain that proved to be an answer to some modern problems At his farm near Parma, Italy, Claudio Grossi offers a visual history of his miracle grain in photos, crackers and loaves. Clara Vannucci Sometime in the early 1990s, Claudio Grossi, a 40-year-old farmer in Parma, in northern Italy, was cleaning his attic when he turned up an old sack full of seeds that he couldn’t identify. The bag, he was sure, had been left by his late great-grandfather, who’d started the farmstead around 1915. Grossi had no idea how long the seeds had been sitting there, deprived of water, soil and sun. Dry and cracked, the kernels looked so old in the palm of his hand that he doubted anything would ever sprout from them. He carried the bag down the stairs, shook the seeds out into a pile of manure and then forgot about them. To his surprise, the seeds soon sprouted a few different types of wheat. One was particularly striking: At six feet high, its plants were about twice as tall as commercial wheat. But the most remarkable feature came when it developed ears—the grain-studded parts at the top of the plant. All of the wheat types Grossi had previously seen grew only one such ear. But the tall wheat grew a full seven ears, always in the same pattern: a long one with six shorties bunched up around it like little fingers. Even the kernels themselves were bigger than those of average wheat. And unlike the typical pale-yellow wheat kernels, they came in a rainbow of colors—yellow, black, red, white and even green, sometimes all on the same stem. Grossi, a grain farmer his whole life, had never seen anything like it. “I thought it was a freak of nature,” he says. He couldn’t find a mention of it in agricultural books. Ears grown from the very first seeds Grossi discovered in his attic. Grossi prizes these first grains, now preserved under glass in his kitchen. Clara Vannucci This article is a selection from the November 2026 issue of Smithsonian magazine For Grossi, a practicing Catholic, the next insight came from a different book altogether. Leafing through a Bible at church one Sunday, he found a passage in the Book of Genesis describing a stalk with seven ears, in a dream that Joseph interprets for the Pharaoh: “And he slept and dreamed the second time: And, behold, seven ears of grain came up upon one stalk, rank and good. And, behold, seven thin ears and blasted with the east wind sprung up after them. And the seven thin ears devoured the seven rank and full ears.” To Grossi, that sounded just like the mysterious crop in his manure pile. “I connected the dots,” Grossi says. That grain must be really ancient , he thought. And if people were farming this odd-looking wheat in biblical times, why does no one today? Back on h

articles.title: TCP Use-After-Free: CVE-2026-98432 / CVSS 9.8
articles.content: Updated October 31, 2026 Red Hat raised its rating to Critical on October 30 and published a mitigation, AlmaLinux has fixed kernels in testing, and Amazon Linux has fixed all of its kernels. The Go Security Team says Go programs open multipath TCP listeners by default, so the setup Anthropic's exploit needs is more common than it first looked. What changed . # Overview Linux's stable kernels shipped a fix on October 11 and 15, 2026 for CVE-2026-98432 , a use-after-free in the IPv4 TCP handshake that a remote, unauthenticated peer can reach. The kernel's own CVE Numbering Authority (CNA) scores it CVSS 3.1 9.8, Critical . The fixed releases are 5.10.272, 5.15.223, 6.1.190, 6.6.159, 6.12.113, 6.18.56, 7.2.10 , and 7.3 , and the bug goes back to Linux 4.4. The upstream fix is a four-line change, but most servers run a distribution's kernel, and as of 5:15 PM CDT, October 31, Ubuntu's tracker still reads "Vulnerable" for its kernel on every release, and Red Hat, which now rates the bug Critical too, lists RHEL 8, 9, and 10 as affected with no fix. Why it's urgent: the bug sits in code every Linux server runs when it accepts an IPv4 TCP connection, before any application sees the connection. Anthropic, whose researcher reported it, says its Claude model wrote a working proof-of-concept exploit that runs commands as root on "Linux servers with a multipath TCP listener," with no credentials. Go programs open those listeners by default, per the Go Security Team. See the timeline . # Key facts Field Detail CVE CVE-2026-98432, "ipv4: free inet_opt and ireq_opt after an RCU grace period," issued by the Linux kernel CNA Severity Critical, CVSS 3.1 9.8 ( AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H ), the kernel CNA's score. Red Hat also rates it Critical, CVSS 3.1 9.8, raised from Important (8.1) on October 30. SUSE rates it important, Ubuntu rates it High, and Oracle and Amazon rate it Important with CVSS 3.1 8.1. Weakness Use-after-free of IPv4 option data during the TCP handshake (the record lists no CWE) Impact Per the CNA's scoring notes: kernel heap contents disclosed to the remote peer, kernel memory corruption, or a crash. Red Hat's bulletin: a remote, unauthenticated attacker "could exploit a race condition during TCP connection request processing to trigger remote code execution." Fixed in 7.2.10 and 6.18.56 (Oct 11) · 6.12.113, 6.6.159, 6.1.190, 5.15.223, and 5.10.272 (Oct 15) · 7.3 (Oct 18) No fix yet Ubuntu (every release) and Red Hat Enterprise Linux (RHEL) 8, 9, and 10, as of 5:15 PM CDT, October 31. AlmaLinux's fixed kernels are still in testing. Upstream branches that reached end-of-life before 5.10 get no fix. Proof of concept Anthropic says Claude built a remote root exploit for servers with a multipath TCP listener. It hasn't published the exploit. CVE records Published on cve.org on October 15. NVD lists it as "Received," with no analysis of its own, as of 5:15 PM CDT, October 31. Credit Reported by Xinyang Ge of Anthropic. Fixed by Eric Dumazet
articles.summary: TCP 释放后使用漏洞 CVE-2026-98432 评分 9.8，Red Hat 升为严重级并发布缓解措施，多家发行版已修复。

articles.title: It's the memory latency, stupid
articles.content: Making GROUP BY faster by doing more (CPU!) work When you see your databases CPU at 100%, what is it actually doing? We like to act as though CPUs run code linearly for simplicity's sake, but in truth CPUs are incredibly complex beasts; they can potentially do many instructions at once, or sometimes none at all (despite our console showing 100%). Because CPUs can do so many things, one CPU at 100% may be doing much less than another at 100%. A CPU is considered "idle" only if no task (Linux task) needs CPU time; this does not mean the CPU itself is being fully saturated. So why would a CPU not be fully utilized, even if it appears to be at 100%? The answer is usually memory . Memory accesses are orders of magnitude slower than internal CPU operations. To give a good picture of how much so, a modern CPU might be able to process somewhere in the realm of 4-8 instructions per nanosecond. A memory access to RAM can take somewhere in the realm of 50-100ns. To ease your mathing, that means a modern CPU can do around 400-800 instructions for every one memory access from RAM. L1 cache ~1 ns ~64 KB · ~4–8 instructions per access L2 cache ~3–4 ns ~1 MB · ~15–30 instructions per access L3 cache ~10–15 ns up to a few hundred MB · ~50–100 instructions per access DRAM ~50–100 ns GBs · ~400–800 instructions per access Given this, CPUs are built from the ground up to work their way around this. The most obvious way this is dealt with is CPU caches. CPU caches keep memory closer to the CPU than RAM, literally baked into the CPU chip. The closest cache (the L1 cache) takes around 1ns per memory operation- that's 50-100x faster than RAM! The "problem" here of course is that the CPU caches are fairly small; the L1 cache for a modern CPU is probably around ~64KB, while the farther caches max out at a few hundred MB for top end processors. A good database tries manipulating data in small "chunks" to take full advantage of caches, and you'll often hear cache utilization as being one of the top concerns of performance engineering. Let's look at GROUP BY aggregations to get a better grip on cache utilization. In GROUP BY, we're looking to take a dataset, group it by a certain column (or more), and perform certain aggregations (for example, count, or sum on another column). The "naive" method might be to open a HashTable keyed by the group key that grows ever larger. For every new row, you would check if that key exists- if it does, go to it's corresponding aggregation and update the result. Simple, right? The problem is that if you have millions of unique groups, you're not utilizing your cache at all! Nearly every HashTable access will be a "cold" hit that goes to RAM. This means that although your CPU may /look/ like it's 100% utilized, in truth it'll constantly be waiting for cold memory accesses. To demonstrate this, we'll take our state-of-the-art Pivot engine and ravage it! We'll remove all our complex logic and replace it with simplicity: fn consume ( & mut self ,
articles.summary: 文章分析数据库 CPU 满载的真正原因是内存延迟，通过增加 CPU 工作量反而可加速 GROUP BY 查询。

articles.title: Do the math: How we took over ChatGPT accounts
articles.content:
In October 2026, we found a way to turn an ordinary public ChatGPT share into attacker-controlled JavaScript running inside the signed-in session of whoever opened it. An attacker could create a malicious conversation, publish it using ChatGPT's normal sharing feature, and send the link to another user. When the victim opened the share, the payload executed as chatgpt.com with access to the victim's authenticated web session. We confirmed that this code could enumerate the victim's conversation list, retrieve content from a private conversation that had never been shared with the attacker, and send data from that conversation to an external server. The payload was not limited to modifying the page or displaying an alert—it could directly call ChatGPT's authenticated APIs as the victim, essentially allowing us to take over the victim's ChatGPT account. The victim did not need to install an App, join a Project, paste code, or open developer tools. Opening the shared link was the only required action. OpenAI fixed the issue on October 26 and classified the report as P1. The chain started with two features that looked harmless on their own: a graph and an HTML Preview. flowchart TD A["Attacker publishes a ChatGPT conversation"] --> B["Victim opens the public share"] B --> C["HTML Preview crosses into the main chatgpt.com page"] C --> D["JavaScript runs in the victim's signed-in session"] D --> E["Any action on chatgpt.com as the victim:
read private chats and files, change the account"] Technical walkthrough It started with a graph and a Preview The question that started this research was simple: if Preview code was boxed into a different website, what could it still talk to? ChatGPT can turn an HTML code block into a small working webpage using its Preview feature. Since that page may contain arbitrary code, ChatGPT sensibly runs it inside a restricted frame on a different web address. The Preview can run JavaScript, but the browser treats it as a different website, so it cannot directly inspect the signed-in ChatGPT page around it. At first, this isolation appeared to work exactly as intended. Code inside the Preview could not read parent.document , which is the main ChatGPT page. That should have been the end of it. The conversation also contained a normal interactive graph. Behind the scenes, the graph loaded a math library called MathLive. Loading it did more than draw the graph: it also installed a listener in the main ChatGPT page for messages related to MathLive's on-screen keyboard. Browsers call the relevant API postMessage . It is a legitimate way for two frames to exchange information even when the browser prevents them from reading each other's pages. You can think of it as a mail slot: the restricted Preview cannot walk into the main page, but it can still drop a message through the slot. That is safe only if the receiver checks who sent the message. MathLive did not make that check for the setting we were interested in. Its listene

articles.title: Switch Lowering in GCC
articles.content: Switch lowering in GCC 2024-01-14 Introduction We have seen in a previous post that switch statements are more complex than they seem. The compiler is able to implement them as a decision tree (even though maybe it shouldn't). Is that everything it can do? In this post, I'll focus on gcc . All optimizations, except the bitset lowering, translate to clang. I'll be using the -O3 optimization flag unless indicated otherwise. I've also slightly edited gcc code and removed certain assertions for brevity. Examples Let us start with a simple example. A function that takes two integers x and val . Depending on the value of x , it calls a corresponding function ( f0 , f1 , and so forth) with val as an argument and returns the result. Were we to implement this manually, we'd would use an array of function pointers, where the input serves as the index into the array. int f0 ( int val ) ; int f1 ( int val ) ; int f2 ( int val ) ; int f3 ( int val ) ; int f4 ( int val ) ; int compact ( int x , int val ) { switch ( x ) { case 0 : return f0 ( val ) ; case 1 : return f1 ( val ) ; case 2 : return f2 ( val ) ; case 3 : return f3 ( val ) ; case 4 : return f4 ( val ) ; default : return 0 ; } return 0 ; } compact: mov eax , edi mov edi , esi cmp eax , 4 ja .L2 jmp [ QWORD PTR .L4 [ 0 + rax * 8 ] ] .L4: .quad .L8 .quad .L7 .quad .L6 .quad .L5 .quad .L3 .L5: jmp f3 .L3: jmp f4 .L8: jmp f0 .L7: jmp f1 .L6: jmp f2 .L2: xor eax , eax ret The compiler agrees with this approach, and transforms the switch statement into a jump table. Moreover, it is able to identify when the values are offset by a constant: int f0 ( int val ) ; int f1 ( int val ) ; int f2 ( int val ) ; int f3 ( int val ) ; int f4 ( int val ) ; int compact ( int x , int val ) { switch ( x ) { case 97 : return f0 ( val ) ; case 98 : return f1 ( val ) ; case 99 : return f2 ( val ) ; case 100 : return f3 ( val ) ; case 101 : return f4 ( val ) ; default : return 0 ; } return 0 ; } compact: lea eax , [ rdi - 97 ] cmp eax , 4 ja .L2 mov edi , esi jmp [ QWORD PTR .L4 [ 0 + rax * 8 ] ] .L4: .quad .L8 .quad .L7 .quad .L6 .quad .L5 .quad .L3 .L5: jmp f3 .L3: jmp f4 .L8: jmp f0 .L7: jmp f1 .L6: jmp f2 .L2: xor eax , eax ret Our intuition suggests that the more sparse the values, the less advantageous the jump table conversion is. Through experimentation, we find that gcc considers the threshold to be around eight jump table entries per case label. In other words, the following function compiles to a jump table: int f0 ( int val ) ; int f1 ( int val ) ; int f2 ( int val ) ; int f3 ( int val ) ; int f4 ( int val ) ; int compact_7 ( int x , int val ) { switch ( x ) { case 0 : return f0 ( val ) ; case 7 : return f1 ( val ) ; case 14 : return f2 ( val ) ; case 21 : return f3 ( val ) ; case 34 : return f4 ( val ) ; default : return 0 ; } return 0 ; } compact_7: mov eax , edi mov edi , esi cmp eax , 34 ja .L2 jmp [ QWORD PTR .L4 [ 0 + rax * 8 ] ] .L4: .quad .L8 .quad .L2 ; ... .quad .L2 .quad .L7 .quad .L2 ; ... .quad .L2 .qua
articles.summary: 文章深入解析 GCC 编译器如何将 switch 语句降低为决策树等多种实现策略及其优化取舍。

articles.title: The Kluever Maneuver
articles.content: In brief, it’s this: whenever you are doing a bugfix, do it in two commits. Write a passing test that exemplifies the buggy behaviour. Fix the bug and also fix the test we just wrote. For example, def add(a, b): return a + b + 1 and through your keen eye you observe that this addition function is buggy. You therefore write a test that records the bad behaviour, Commit 1 diff --git a/test_arith.py b/test_arith.py --- a/test_arith.py +++ b/test_arith.py @@ -0,0 +1,2 @@ +def test_add(a, b): + assert add(2, 2) == 5 Then comes the bugfix, Commit 2 diff --git a/arith.py b/arith.py --- a/arith.py +++ b/arith.py @@ -1,2 +1,2 @@ def add(a, b): - return a + b + 1 + return a + b diff --git a/test_arith.py b/test_arith.py --- a/test_arith.py +++ b/test_arith.py @@ -1,2 +1,2 @@ def test_add(a, b): - assert add(2, 2) == 5 + assert add(2, 2) == 4 BUT Y THO Two reasons: Demonstrable proof that the bugfix actually fixed the bug CI still passes at every commit The traditional way to do this is to do a bugfix and add a test in the same commit. But what if the test accidentally already passed before the alleged bugfix and the alleged bugfix didn’t actually work? In that case the added test gives false confidence that the bugfix worked. Alright, show me Here’s a less obvious example. Suppose we want to make sure users are not underage, def age_in_years(birthday, today): return today.year - birthday.year def can_access(birthday, today): return 18 <= age_in_years( birthday, today ) You notice that this age check is buggy. It’s only considering the years. If it’s October 2026, but you were born on December 2008, you are not 18 yet. To fix it, the problem is just an off-by-one. diff --git a/dates.py b/dates.py --- a/dates.py +++ b/dates.py @@ -4,7 +4,7 @@ def age_in_years(birthday, today): return today.year - birthday.year def can_access(birthday, today): - return 18 <= age_in_years( + return 18 < age_in_years( birthday, today ) diff --git a/test_date.py b/test_date.py --- a/test_date.py +++ b/test_date.py @@ -0,0 +1,5 @@ +def test_can_access(): + assert can_access( + date(2007, 1, 1), + date(2026, 1, 1) + ) The astute reader will observe the problem isn’t in the can_access function but in the age calculation. The bugfix isn’t an actual bugfix and the proposed test actually passes both before and after the proposed fix. The Kluever Maneuver would have prevented this. We wrongly check that someone born on New Year’s Eve in 2008 is eighteen on New Year’s Day in 2026. commit 1 diff --git a/test_date.py b/test_date.py --- a/test_date.py +++ b/test_date.py @@ -0,0 +1,5 @@ +def test_can_access(): + assert can_access( + date(2008, 12, 31), + date(2026, 1, 1) + ) Then we fix the age calculation and flip the test. commit 2 diff --git a/dates.py b/dates.py --- a/dates.py +++ b/dates.py @@ -1,7 +1,10 @@ +from dateutil.relativedelta import relativedelta def age_in_years(birthday, today): - return today.year - birthday.year + return relativedelta( + today, + birthday + ).years def ca
articles.summary: 文章提出“Kluever 手法”：修复 bug 时拆成两次提交，先写一个能复现错误行为的通过测试，再修复 bug 并同步修正测试。

articles.title: Avoid Public Functions Calling Other Public Functions
articles.content: Avoid Public Functions Calling Other Public Functions Oct 29, 2026 A small-scale rule of thumb. This article will land much better with a concrete example, but I am drawing a blank here, so you gotta just blindly trust my say so! When implementing a software module, it’s often a case that you are writing a public function foo , and at least part of what foo does is already handled by another public function bar . The DRY instinct encourages you to call bar() from within foo . This usually creates problems down the line. Instead, create a new private function and refactor both foo and bar to call that shared helper: // BAD pub fn foo () void { return bar(.{ .frobnicate = true }); } pub fn bar (options: struct { frobnicate: bool = false , }) void { // ... } // GOOD pub fn foo () void { return helper(.frobnicate); } pub fn bar () void { return helper(.transmogrify); } fn helper (mode: enum { frobnicate, transmogrify }) void { // ... } Rationale: the goal of a public API is to provide an interface that works best at the call site. If parts of public API are re-used to implement the rest of the API, then there’s a tension between making the interface convenient for the outside user and making it convenient to use from within abstraction itself. Namely, functions tend to grow optional parameters that should never be set by the user. Crucially, the parameter growth and interface degradation can happen after the original code sharing. By proactively making the shared implementation private, the tension is defused. You still might need to tinker with helper signature until it does everything it needs to do, but, because the helper is private, this is a cheap, local change. A notable exception to this rule of thumb are “shortcut” APIs, where a public function is defined as a commonly used chain of calls to other public functions. There, the rule is the opposite — no private calls are allowed, to make sure that it is a genuine shortcut, and not a midlayer mistake. P.S. While researching if anyone wrote a better blog post already, I stumbled upon a fun stack overflow question, asking, paraphrasing: I’ve heard that it is bad when a public function calls another public function. Is this really so? The most upvoted answer explains that it is indeed bad, because this makes mocking to test a single method in isolation more complicated. Which is, imo, a natural, but horrible consequence of misguided approach to testing. You shouldn’t be mocking your methods, you should mock your IO. And, similarly, you shouldn’t test methods, but rather software functionality (unless you are building a public library with a stable API, which is a fun and important, but very narrow fraction of software development). The accepted answer says that this recommendation makes no sense if it is not backed by an industry wide or an organizational standard. Which somehow manages to make even less sense — you shouldn’t follow the guideline rules because they are written in sanctified ink! R
articles.summary: 作者提出一条小经验法则：模块实现中应避免公共函数直接调用其他公共函数，以降低耦合、便于测试与维护。

articles.title: The support case of a customer who said that all they could see was a black screen
articles.content: If you hold a PC’s power button for 12 seconds, it will turn off at the hardware level without notifying the operating system. This is a safety feature so that you can turn of the computer even if the operating system’s “Shut down” command isn’t working. After eight seconds of the power button being held down, the Windows kernel realizes that the user is trying to do a force-power-off of the system, and it quickly takes a kernel dump that can be uploaded to the Windows Error Reporting service the next time you turn the system on. (Sometimes four seconds isn’t enough time to get enough information, and the kernel dump is incomplete. I believe that on Windows Insider builds of Windows, you get a message that says something like “Please let go of the power button so we can collect more information, and then we will turn off the computer.” This gives the kernel more time to finish capturing its kernel dump.) These emergency kernel dumps are internally classified as “long power button hold” (LPBH) failures. One of the pieces of information recorded in these emergency kernel dumps is whether the screen consists entirely of black pixels. Those failures are sub-classified as “black screen LPBH”, and they go to a special virtual team for analysis. (I happen to be a member of this black screen LPBH team.) Sometimes the problem is a broken video driver. Sometimes the video driver is doing just fine, but the desktop compositor is just handing black pixels to the video driver. Sometimes the desktop compositor is doing just fine, but nobody is drawing anything to the screen. And those cases are further subdivided further into cases like “there is nobody around to draw anything” or “the person who normally draws stuff is hung.” Back in the Windows 3.1 days, there was a customer product support call that would today have been classified as a “black screen” bug: The customer reported that they turned on the computer, and Windows started up, but when the logo went away, all they saw was a blank screen. After some questioning, the customer support engineer put the story together: It turned out that this customer really liked the color black, so they decided to set up a goth theme. They set the wallpaper color to black. They set the title bar color to black. They set the button color to black. They set the window background color to black. They set the window text color to black. Every possible color you could pick in the Colors control panel was set to black. Once you get yourself into this situation, it’s hard to get out because you can’t see anything. I don’t know how the customer support engineer fixed the problem, but I’m guessing that they booted into MS-DOS, ran EDIT.COM , and deleted the [colors] section from the win.ini file , thereby returning all the system colors to defaults.
articles.summary: 文章讲述一起客服案例：客户只看到黑屏，最终发现与长按电源键 12 秒触发硬件级强制关机有关。

articles.title: How hard is it to check for whitespace?
articles.content: How hard is it to check for whitespace? When looking through a piece of source code recently, I stumbled across this method from Guava – a popular Java library from Google. As you might've guessed from the name, this method checks whether a given character is a whitespace character. Yet the code looks a lot more complex than a simple c == ' ' check. This made me curious and sent me down a small rabbit hole trying to understand where all this complexity was coming from. If you're curious how this code works too, this article is for you. What is whitespace, anyway? The first thing one needs when inspecting a function that checks whether a character is whitespace is to define what whitespace actually is. While the SPACE (U+0020) is probably the best-known whitespace character, it's not the only one. If you've been writing code for a while, you can probably name a few more – the non-breaking space NO-BREAK SPACE (U+00A0) , a tab CHARACTER TABULATION (U+0009) , a newline LINE FEED (U+000A) . Well, there are more. Unicode defines a White_Space property that gives us a list of 25 characters. Here they are – meticulously copied , , , , , , , , , , , , , , , , , , , , , , , , . Each of these characters has a different purpose. FIGURE SPACE (U+2007) , for example, has the same width as a digit in a table, while THIN SPACE (U+2009) and HAIR SPACE (U+200A) provide progressively smaller gaps. NO-BREAK SPACE (U+00A0) has the width of an ordinary space, but keeps the surrounding text together when wrapping a line. It's not always easy to tell whether a character is in the whitespace set from the name or by looking at the glyph either. For instance, ZERO WIDTH SPACE (U+200B) isn't a whitespace character at all. Despite the name, it's a format character that can indicate a word or line break opportunity without adding a visible gap. There are also some less obvious members of the set too. OGHAM SPACE MARK (U+1680) can actually be rendered as a visible horizontal line. In Ogham fonts with a stemline, the space continues that line between letters (e.g. ᚛ᚆᚓᚂᚂᚑ ᚒᚑᚏᚂᚇ᚜), while in stemless fonts, it's blank. So even the assumption that whitespace must look empty isn't always true. Different runtimes, different rules Having a single definition of whitespace is only useful if everyone can agree on it. But even within a single runtime, some libraries might disagree on what whitespace is. Consider the NO-BREAK SPACE (U+00A0) I mentioned above. It's included in Unicode's White_Space property, but Java explicitly excludes it , along with two other non-breaking spaces. The javadoc usefully highlights that the method checks for whitespace according to Java , rather than according to the Unicode property we had a look at before. Character.isWhitespace( ' ' ); // true Character.isWhitespace( '\u00A0' ); // false But what about other runtimes? Looking at two more popular ones, Python and JavaScript, we can see that there isn't a single authoritative list of characters everyone ag

articles.title: No, npm, “estee” is not a typo of “testem”
articles.content: No, npm, “estee” is not a typo of “testem” Oct. 30, 2026 So, alright, look, here's the thing. Storyteller has a really long npm namespace because “storyteller” is a really common word, and so “@storyteller/” was already taken (by someone who doesn’t actually seem to use it, which, if you’re reading this, I’m still interested in your namespace!). So we’re stuck with “@storyteller-platform/”, and that means our command line tool for book forced alignment is named “@storyteller-platform/align”, and so you need to run “npx @storyteller-platform/align --help”, etc, which is a handful! And so we came up with a cute nickname, “estee” (get it? Storyteller -> ST -> estee?), and we were pretty happy with it, so I went to publish a v0.0.1 to npm so I could set up Trusted Publishing with our GitLab repo and then this happened: 403 Forbidden - PUT https://registry.npmjs.org/estee - Package name too similar to existing packages espree,testem ... What? Too similar to... “testem”? I mean I can almost understand “espree”. I don’t actually see how someone could accidentally typo “espree” as “estee”, but at least they're similarly shaped. But “testem”? No chance, that is not a typo candidate for “estee”. I mean it’s pretty clear what’s happening here. Npm is using a Levenshtein distance calculation and banning any packages that have a Levenshtein distance of 2 or less from existing popular package names. Levenshtein distance counts the number of “edits” needed to get from one string to another, where an edit is a single character insertion, replacement, or deletion. So to get from “estee” to “testem”, we have to make the following edits: t estee t este e m See? Levenshtein distance of 2. We used this for the first several iterations of the Storyteller algorithm, which needs to find where a given sentence lives in a transcription of an audiobook. Here’s the thing: Levenshtein doesn't scale down very well. You can’t just set a single threshold for all input lengths, because as the length of the string approaches the threshold, the proportion of the set of valid strings covered by the threshold explodes. Here’s what I mean. Say you are concerned with all npm package names with length 4. Npm allows the characters a-z, plus the symbols “.”, “-”, and “_”, so there are 29 possible characters in our alphabet. For a 4-character string, that gives us 29 4 possible names, or 707,281 possible names. But what happens if you don't allow any names that have a Levenshtein distance of 2 from any existing names? How many packages can exist before you have to start rejecting all new package names? This is a little hard to answer completely (and we’re ignoring the fact that, because Levenshtein distance allows pure insertions and deletions, this also affects 2-, 3-, 5-, and 6-character names), but we can set an upper bound: 29 2 , or 841. This is because, since Levenshtein distance allows a replace edit, you can get from a string like “abaa” to any string starting with “ab”. So once y

articles.title: Mystery of 60-Second Fluctuations in Power Grids Solved
articles.content: Mystery of 60-Second Fluctuations in Power Grids Solved 30 October 2026 Why do our grids show a brief spike in electricity demand every minute? A team led by Dirk Witthaut from Forschungszentrum Jülich has now demonstrated that this is due to regular power checks carried out by large-scale battery storage systems. These findings could help to make our electricity supply more robust, as the team reports in an article published in Nature Energy . Copyright: Regine Panknin Tennet Germany, the largest transmission system operator in Germany, has observed over several years that the frequency in the European power grid dips briefly every 60 seconds. While these deviations were not critical to grid security, they were clearly measurable and unusually regular. The cause of this phenomenon was initially unclear. A team from Jülich led by Dirk Witthaut, together with researchers from the University of Cologne and the Karlsruhe Institute of Technology, set out to investigate – and found the answer: the cause appears to be the many large-scale battery storage systems that check their state of charge every minute. This leads to measurable fluctuations in electricity consumption, which can contribute to turbine wear and tear, for example. The battery storage systems ensure an uninterrupted power supply, and their numbers have increased significantly worldwide in recent years. The researchers found that this was not a European phenomenon, but a global one. Many devices, a common rhythm “It really was years of detective work,” says Witthaut. The grid frequency pattern is shaped by many different factors. For example, it reveals the influence of electricity trading, with power stations being switched on and off abruptly, as well as the fluctuating feed-in from renewable energy sources, and various other disturbances. Uns war schnell klar, dass es sich bei der Ursache um etwas handeln muss, das von der Uhr gesteuert wird Prof. Dr. Dirk Witthaut, Leiter des Departments Netzwerke und komplexe Systeme, Institut für Energiesystemtechnik (ICE-1) “It quickly became clear to us that the cause must be something controlled by the clock,” says Witthaut. There was no other way to explain the precise 60-second cycle. It was also clear that: “The observed effect can only be produced if many devices are consuming electricity at the same time.” A single consumer or generator could therefore be ruled out. Measurements on campus provide the clue But how do all these devices synchronize their consumption? The researchers finally found the crucial clues with the help of the Living Lab Energy Campus. This research infrastructure on the Jülich campus is primarily used to develop and test highly integrated energy supply systems. articles.title: Pile-ins, payouts, and pacing pressure: the investors behind the VCs open up
articles.content: The limited partners who provide the capital to venture firms — the “money behind the money” — are feeling great right now. They’re in uncharted territory in many ways, but also potentially exceedingly lucrative territory. Normally, LPs typically spread their bets across many firms to diversify their own portfolios. They write checks to emerging managers and established ones, to generalist firms and specialists. The goal is a strong return, but also to minimize risk. That’s the typical playbook. But typical is out the window. OpenAI and Anthropic’s valuations have shot up so quickly that nearly everyone has piled into the same two companies on the way up, often inside the same venture firm, despite the longstanding venture convention of avoiding investments that conflict with one another. No one is complaining, either. The LPs I speak with seem unbothered by this big gamble, given the potential returns; they’re expecting a bonanza. But they do see danger ahead, even if they describe this as a “yellow light” situation, and they’re uneasy about how quickly VCs are coming back to raise new funds. I talked about all of it recently with Beezer Clarkson of LGT Capital Partners, a Zurich-based diversified asset manager, and Amit Bhatti of TrueBridge, a Chapel Hill firm that focuses solely on venture. This conversation has been edited for length. These are strange days — exciting but also scary. How are you feeling about your roles right now, and your place in this startup ecosystem? Beezer Clarkson: It’s very busy, but I wouldn’t say it’s scary. There’s a lot of change and a lot of variables at play. I love venture, so I find the chaos fun. I’ve been doing this for a couple of decades, so seeing the cycles makes it less scary. You appreciate that these things happen, and that we should enjoy the upside, because sometimes there’s downside, and the up is a lot more fun than the down. Amit Bhatti: If anything, it’s exciting. Venture is sometimes looked at as a niche, and now that AI is all-consuming, all the attention is on venture. This feels like our moment more than it is like, “Oh gosh, what’s going to happen?” The pace of investing and the valuations may be different, but really meaningful stuff is happening, and all the attention is focused on this corner of private equity. Your funds all hold the same brands now, OpenAI and Anthropic, multiplied across however many funds you back, and your job is to keep your institutions diversified. How do you think about that? Obviously it’s great right now, but if things turned, it would be less great. Amit Bhatti: Venture has always been a power law business, so I actually view the concentration as a good thing. If we were getting to the maturity of one of our funds and there were still lots of tiny positions, something’s gone wrong. Our funds that are 10-plus years old are starting to consolidate into a few names. There’s a lot of Databricks, a lot of SpaceX, a lot of Stripe. In this generation of funds, I wou
articles.summary: 为风投提供资金的有限合伙人表示当前处境极佳，虽进入未知领域但潜在回报丰厚。

articles.title: Cloudflare’s Post-Quantum GeoKey Manager Enters Closed Beta Without Attribute-Based Encryption
articles.content: Cloudflare has moved a post-quantum rebuild of GeoKey Manager into closed beta, guarding geo-fenced keys with hybrid ML-KEM-768 and X25519 instead of the attribute-based encryption used since 2022. Keys live only in kernel memory on verified regional servers, and any failed check rejects the request, a fail-closed choice practitioners ask could cause a regional outage. GA is planned for Q1 2027. By Steef-Jan Wiggers
articles.summary: Cloudflare将后量子版GeoKey Manager推入封闭测试，改用混合ML-KEM-768与X25519保护地理围栏密钥。

articles.title: OpenBSD 8.0 Brings Expanded Hardware Support, Security Enhancements, and Virtualization Improvements
articles.content: OpenBSD 8.0 is a substantial upgrade bringing broader hardware compatibility, enhanced security, an expanded virtual address space, and support for modern architectures, including Intel Arc A-Series graphics support, ARM64 hibernation, RISC-V improvements, and enhanced virtual machine support. By Sergio De Simone
articles.summary: OpenBSD 8.0发布，扩展硬件兼容性、增强安全与虚拟化，支持Intel Arc显卡、ARM64休眠及RISC-V改进。

articles.content: There was a flurry of activity during the week of October 19th, 2026, highlighting: first release candidates of: Spring Boot, Spring Framework, Spring Data, Spring Cloud, Spring Security, Spring for GraphQL, Spring Session, Spring Integration, Spring HATEOS, Spring Modulith, Spring REST Docs, Spring AI, Spring Batch, Spring AMQP, Spring for Apache Kafka, Spring LDAP and Spring Web Services. articles.title: Kubernetes Confidential Containers Get Fortanix Attestation and Key Management
articles.content: Fortanix's CoCo integration connects workload attestation to decryption-key release for Kubernetes AI workloads. GPU-verification settings affect protection, while upstream Trustee and Azure Secure Key Release offer alternative routes to attestation-based key release. By Mark Silvester
articles.summary: Fortanix为Kubernetes机密容器集成证明与密钥管理，将工作负载证明与解密密钥释放绑定。

articles.title: LocalStack for Azure Enters Public Preview with Security Settings Stored but Not Enforced
articles.content: LocalStack has opened its Azure emulator to a free public preview, running Azure services locally and accepting existing ARM, Bicep, and Terraform without rewrites. Its own documentation reports partial operation coverage per service and a consistent pattern: configuration is stored and returned, while enforcement of access restrictions, TLS, and network rules is not implemented. By Steef-Jan Wiggers
articles.summary: LocalStack推出Azure模拟器公开预览，可本地运行Azure服务并兼容ARM、Bicep与Terraform，但部分功能仅存储不生效。

articles.title: Google Discloses PageBreak AI Security Agent That Found 500+ XSS Bugs
articles.content: According to a paper published by Google, its AI-powered security agent has uncovered more than 500 XSS vulnerabilities across its web applications since entering full operation in January. PageBreak uses Gemini models to autonomously investigate potential vulnerabilities, but reports them only after deterministic validators successfully reproduce the exploit against a running application. By Renato Losio
articles.summary: 谷歌披露AI安全代理PageBreak，自1月全面运行以来已发现500多个XSS漏洞，基于Gemini自主调查。

articles.title: DoorDash Cuts Grocery Reorder Latency from 16 to 2 Seconds with AI Agents
articles.content: DoorDash reduced grocery reorder latency from 16 to 2 seconds by precomputing recurring purchase needs using batch LLM inference and deterministic validation. Live catalog resolution keeps product selections current, while an editable shopping interface avoids unnecessary model calls. The company reports that shopping list views doubled and the flow’s order rate increased by approximately 34% By Leela Kumili
articles.summary: DoorDash利用批量LLM推理与确定性校验预计算复购需求，将杂货重下单延迟从16秒降至2秒。

articles.title: Netflix Treats GPU Reliability as a Distributed Systems Problem
articles.content: Netflix has detailed how it is building a reliability platform for large-scale GPU training and inference, using layered health checks, automated remediation, and fault-tolerant training to keep jobs running despite hardware failures. By Craig Risi
articles.summary: Netflix将GPU可靠性视为分布式系统问题，通过分层健康检查、自动修复与容错训练保障大规模任务。

articles.title: Presentation: The Ladder Is Missing Rungs: Engineering Progression When AI Ate the Middle
articles.content: Alasdair Allan discusses empirical research from METR and Anthropic on AI coding adoption. He explains the "supervision paradox," where reliance on AI tools disrupts junior skill development, risks institutional context loss, and threatens the long-term engineering pipeline needed to oversee autonomous systems effectively. By Alasdair Allan
articles.summary: 演讲探讨AI编码普及下的“监督悖论”：依赖AI工具削弱初级工程师技能成长，威胁长期工程人才梯队。

articles.title: Netflix Titus Adds Single-Tenant VM Isolation for Containers
articles.content: Netflix has added single-tenant Titus, a mode that runs one task alone on its own right-sized EC2 instance. The Compute/Platform team still owns and patches the host, so application teams keep the same API and deployment path By Claudio Masolo
articles.summary: Netflix 为 Titus 容器平台新增单租户模式，任务独占定制 EC2 实例，平台团队仍负责主机维护，应用团队 API 与部署方式不变。

articles.title: AI Weekly Issue #541: Big Tech reports AI spending Wednesday as CoreWeave debt hits distress
articles.content: This issue looks ahead. On Wednesday the Fed announces its rate decision, then Microsoft and Alphabet report after the close. Amazon follows on Thursday. Investors want to know whether AI spending is still paying off, and the credit market is already nervous: insurance against a CoreWeave default now costs more than 10% a year. Anthropic is expected to file its IPO paperwork publicly any day. Moonshot says Kimi K3.1 Pro's open weights arrive November 4. Israel votes on Tuesday after a campaign full of AI deepfakes, and the US midterms are a week from Tuesday. In the middle: so far, AI has paid off for the companies that sell it, not the ones that buy it.
articles.summary: AI Weekly 关注微软、Alphabet、亚马逊本周财报，投资者质疑 AI 支出回报，CoreWeave 违约保险成本飙升显示信贷市场紧张。

articles.title: AI Weekly Issue #540: AI is finding software flaws faster than teams can fix them
articles.content: This Applied AI edition looks at what organizations actually did with AI over the past two weeks, drawn from our Use-Case Library and from SEC filings. Three things stand out: AI now finds security flaws at record volume, AI agents do a large share of the work at some companies, and test agents keep doing things nobody asked them to do.
articles.summary: AI Weekly 应用版指出企业用 AI 发现安全漏洞的速度已超过修复速度，部分公司大量工作由 AI 代理完成，测试代理持续运行。

articles.title: AI Weekly Issue #539: AI-made midterm ads top $137 million, and 70% carry no AI label
articles.content: Campaigns and PACs have spent more than $137 million on AI-generated or AI-enhanced midterm ads, and about 70% of them carry no AI label, the New York Times reported. The biggest pro-AI super PAC network paid about $20 million to a Nevada company that exists only as a post office box. A new report found 81 of 134 AI models failed a test built from terrorist-style questions. A video game reverse engineering site is closing because AI made the work too easy. Some companies that rushed into AI are now limiting it, and a JAMA study counted 270 million questions doctors asked one AI tool. In the middle: police in Michigan used an AI-generated photo of a teenager to catch a suspect.
articles.summary: 据纽约时报报道，竞选团队和 PAC 在 AI 生成中期选举广告上花费超 1.37 亿美元，约 70% 未标注 AI 生成。

articles.title: AI Weekly Issue #537: AI models may soon copy themselves onto smart fridges, Anthropic says
articles.content: This issue is built from the links the AI experts we follow shared most since our last issue on October 8, minus the stories we already sent you in the Daily Espresso. The most shared: Anthropic's warning that small AI models may soon be able to copy themselves onto home devices. Also: a large study of what AI coding agents change at real companies, a fight over how to check AI math proofs, creative workers pushing back on AI, and police buying more AI.
articles.summary: Anthropic 警告小型 AI 模型可能很快能自我复制到智能冰箱等家用设备，成为本周 AI 专家分享最多的消息。

articles.title: AI Weekly Issue #536: Top AI models failed a test of inventing new AI research
articles.content: This issue is built from the links the AI experts we follow shared over the past three days. Most of them look ahead: whether AI can do AI research on its own, who gets a say in governing it, how it is moving into war planning, and how it is moving onto personal computers.
articles.summary: AI Weekly 汇总专家关注点：顶尖 AI 模型未能通过自主开展 AI 研究的测试，同时探讨 AI 治理、军事规划与个人电脑应用。

articles.title: AI Weekly Issue #535: AI got too expensive, so companies are moving to cheaper models
articles.content: This Applied AI edition looks at what organizations actually did with AI over the past three weeks. Three patterns stand out: companies switching models to control cost, large deployments that are now in daily use, and a growing list of places where AI was restricted or removed.
articles.summary: AI Weekly 应用版发现企业因 AI 成本过高而转向更便宜的模型，大型部署进入日常使用，同时 AI 受限或被撤除的场景增多。

articles.title: AI Weekly Issue #534: Universities cannot grade their way out of AI
articles.content: This week, campus IT leaders voted AI their top priority for the first time, Cambridge refused Turnitin's new terms over AI training on student work, Dartmouth opened an investigation into its own provost's writing, and Ken Griffin gave Carnegie Mellon $3 billion. Student AI use is no longer a future scenario. The useful question for universities is whether they can teach students to work with AI and still certify what those students can do without it. New evidence from tutoring trials, assessment redesigns, student-support systems and campus data deals points to a practical answer.
articles.summary: 高校 IT 负责人首次将 AI 列为首要任务，剑桥拒绝 Turnitin 新条款，达特茅斯调查教务长写作，AI 使用已非未来议题。

articles.title: AI Weekly Issue #533: Meta tested human callers behind its AI phone agent
articles.content: The AI story of September 22–28 was not simply that agents became more capable. It was that their hidden handoffs became visible: a supposedly automated call could reach a contractor, a supposedly private prompt or image could reach a reviewer, a monitor could detect an agent long before a person stopped it, and a local app flaw could inherit every permission a user had granted. The new AI Weekly Who’s Who census points to one practical question: when an agent crosses a boundary, who knows—and who can still intervene?
articles.summary: AI Weekly 指出 AI 代理的隐藏人工转接被曝光：自动电话可转给外包人员，私密提示或图像可能被审核员看到。

articles.title: AI Weekly Issue #531: AI labs shipped agents before agreeing how to report failures
articles.content: The AI story of September 14–20 was not one spectacular model launch. It was the machinery around agents becoming visible: people reading private chats, models writing instructions into their own memory, plugins updating beneath users, and regulators asking how to stop a system after release. The latest AI Weekly Who’s Who census surfaced 535 expert-shared links. We ranked them by consequence and reader relevance, not by raw share count. Here is what mattered last week—and, more importantly, what could move the story from September 22–28.
articles.summary: AI Weekly 报道 AI 实验室在未就故障报告方式达成一致前就发布代理，暴露人工阅读私聊、模型写入自身记忆、插件静默更新等问题。

articles.title: AI Weekly Issue #530: Applied AI This Week
articles.content: Companies are giving AI specific jobs: checking security cameras, helping farmers understand their records, searching satellite images, and preparing sales quotes. This edition explains how those tools work, who can use them, and what companies have reported so far.
articles.summary: 企业为 AI 分配具体任务：检查监控摄像头、帮助农民理解记录、搜索卫星图像、准备销售报价，本期介绍其原理与使用情况。

articles.title: The future is Postgres
articles.content: Craig Kerstiens returns to talk about the ever-expanding world of Postgres: a deliberately boring core, a thriving extension ecosystem, and pg_lake bringing DuckDB and Iceberg into the mix. We dig into the pain of ETL, what Craig is watching in Postgres 19, the impact of AI on open source maintainers, and why the database still has plenty of room to grow.
articles.summary: Craig Kerstiens 谈 Postgres 生态：核心刻意保持简单，扩展生态繁荣，pg_lake 引入 DuckDB 和 Iceberg，并讨论 ETL 痛点与 AI 对维护者的影响。

articles.title: Building what's next
articles.content: This week I'm talking with Zeno Rocha, CEO of Resend, about scaling "boring" email to 3 million users, the secret Go rewrite behind it, and building for agents. We cover pricing.md, MCP, spam gangs, and why Resend keeps what's next for email.
articles.summary: Resend CEO Zeno Rocha 谈将“无聊”的邮件服务扩展到 300 万用户、背后的 Go 重写、为代理构建，以及定价与反垃圾策略。

articles.title: From zero to NanoClaw
articles.content: Gavriel Cohen, creator of NanoClaw and co-founder of NanoCo, joins Adam to explain how a 40-hour weekend project became a viral open source hit and the foundation of an enterprise AI company. Gavriel describes the security concerns that led him to build a small, container-isolated alternative to OpenClaw, why he released it under the MIT license, and why the project's community and credibility are more valuable than keeping its code private. They explore the shift from writing code to architecting the environments in which agents work, NanoClaw's "skills over features" approach, the approval and governance layers required inside large companies, and a future where every worker manages agents without surrendering human judgment. They close with the technical simplicity behind NanoClaw, containers, TypeScript, SQLite, and a two-database design, and Adam's case for durable Agent Flow artifacts that keep organizational context from disappearing into chat.
articles.summary: NanoClaw 作者 Gavriel Cohen 讲述 40 小时周末项目如何成为病毒式开源爆款，并因安全顾虑打造容器隔离的 OpenAI 替代方案。

articles.title: Forking Cal.com to closed source
articles.content: This week I'm joined by Peer Richelsen, co-founder of Cal.com. What if the majority of open source repositories are already compromised and we just don't know it yet? That's the theory Peer brings to the table this week. We dig into how AI has flattened the knowledge graph to the point that a 16-year-old can vibe hack a power station just as easily as their mom can vibe code an iOS app, why the reporting culture that has kept open source safe all these years is collapsing under AI generated noise, Cal.com's move to fork its own codebase and take the sensitive parts private, and the eye opening reality that shipping "$1 of AI tokens for pennies on the dollar" is now a common startup business model.
articles.summary: Cal.com 联合创始人 Peer Richelsen 提出多数开源仓库可能已被攻陷的猜想，并讨论 AI 如何压平知识图谱及项目转向闭源。

articles.title: Postgres at PlanetScale
articles.content: Sam Lambert is back after 4 years and he does not hold back! We cover $5 PlanetScale Postgres, the Neki "do-over" of Vitess, agents shipping schema changes through deploy requests, rolling back a 500TB table in seconds, and the very real question of whether to open source any of it. Plus: why he thinks the sleeping, lazy giants should be broken up.
articles.summary: PlanetScale 的 Sam Lambert 谈 5 美元 Postgres、Vitess 重做、代理通过部署请求提交 schema 变更，以及秒级回滚 500TB 表。

articles.title: Canary tokens and digital tripwires
articles.content: Haroon Meer is back! Haroon is the Founder of Thinkst, the ~50-person bootstrapped company behind Canary and Canarytokens — honeypots and tripwires you sprinkle inside your network and forget about until an attacker touches one. We talk about the AWS API key token attackers just can't resist trying, the real credit card token backed by an actual bank partnership, Breadcrumbs (their brand-new feature that leads intruders straight to your canaries), a live demo where a hardware Canary becomes a Synology NAS in one click, and how a company with zero outbound sales and no price increase in ten years quietly passed $22.5 million in ARR.
articles.summary: Thinkst 创始人 Haroon Meer 谈 Canary 蜜罐与数字绊线，包括攻击者难以抗拒的 AWS API 密钥诱饵，公司仅约 50 人且自筹资金。

articles.title: From open source hits to OpenAI
articles.content: This week I'm talking with Max Stoiber, currently working on ChatGPT's plugin directory and app platform at OpenAI. We discuss the hundreds of open source projects nobody remembers alongside the big ones like react-boilerplate and styled-components, how Spectrum became part of GitHub and eventually helped shape GitHub Discussions, the founder growth that came from building Stellate, the GraphQL cache that turned into a dual acquisition by Shopify and The Guild, and why ChatGPT apps feel like a new surface for software.
articles.summary: 现于 OpenAI 负责 ChatGPT 插件目录与应用平台的 Max Stoiber 回顾 react-boilerplate、styled-components 等开源项目及 Spectrum 并入 GitHub 的历程。

articles.title: MCP on Code Mode
articles.content: This week I'm talking with Matt Carey about Code Mode and how most of us have been thinking about MCP all wrong. Matt works on the Agents SDK and MCP at Cloudflare — we discuss how server-side Code Mode lets one MCP server expose all ~2,500 Cloudflare API endpoints in about 1,000 tokens of context, the dynamic Worker loader that runs model-written code safely in a V8 isolate, Matt's own workflow with Claude, where memory fits into the future of agents, and his Zaggy git wrapper that keeps agents from force-pushing his repos.
articles.summary: Cloudflare 的 Matt Carey 谈 Code Mode：服务端模式让单个 MCP 服务器以约 1000 token 上下文暴露全部约 2500 个 Cloudflare API 端点。

articles.title: Automation at the speed of Swamp
articles.content: This week I'm talking with Adam Jacob, founder of System Initiative and creator of Swamp, about what happens when AI agents change the entire shape of software development. We discuss how he went from an 18-person team down to five and shipped Swamp 900 times in four weeks, why he brought User Acceptance Testing (UAT) testing back from the 90s, why software architecture (and domain-driven design) suddenly matters more than knowing how to write code, the live demo where I pointed Swamp at my Proxmox box and watched it write its own automation (blew my mind!!), and why he'll never accept a pull request to Swamp, ever.
articles.summary: System Initiative 创始人 Adam Jacob 分享 AI 代理如何重塑软件开发，团队从18人缩减至5人，四周内交付 Swamp 900次。

articles.title: Binance Replenishes 90% of Stolen $6.3B, Pledges They'll Cover It All, Reopen Sunday
articles.content: "We've now replenished 90% of the stolen assets, and we're committed to covering the remaining 10%," Binance co-CEO Richard Teng posted on X, adding that "Our users will not bear the financial impact of this incident." "Binance said it was able to replace the funds taken in the record hack by using company money to buy new tokens," reports NBC News: The remaining 10% consists of tokens that are less liquid, meaning they may take longer to buy, it said in a statement posted on X... Binance said it has set aside around $6.34 billion of company funds internally to cover the losses. The money spent re-buying tokens came from using part of its $1 billion Secure Asset Fund for Users, a bitcoin reserve it holds to protect customers in the event of security breaches, as well as some of its Futures Insurance Fund, and the company's own corporate treasury, it said on X. NBC News reports that the FBI blames the breach on a North Korea-sponsored group known as TraderTraitor: Members of [TraderTraitor] were observed by law enforcement converting stolen assets into the cryptocurrency ethereum, the FBI said in a statement, adding that it expects "further laundering" of the assets through the use of related technology... After the hack, the exchange stopped allowing customers to withdraw their funds, but it said Saturday it was still on track to reopen withdrawals Sunday. CNBC reports: The world's largest crypto exchange initially said the hack may involve "a compromised DevOps engineer's laptop, which allowed an attacker to gain access to a service container and submit unauthorized withdrawal transactions." However, Co-CEO Richard Teng later said the attack involved a more complex process rather than the misuse of a single engineer's permissions. The New York Times describes what happened when Binance first spotted "a multibillion-dollar deluge of digital coins" pouring out of its accounts: As the news spread, Binance's top executives put together an informal war room on Wea, the
articles.summary: 币安已补回被盗63亿美元资产的90%，承诺覆盖剩余部分，用户不受财务影响，平台周日恢复运营。

articles.title: Computer Simulations Suggest Building Blocks of Life Didn't Arrive on Prehistoric Comets
articles.content: CNN reports: The popular theory that comets were crucial in kick-starting life on Earth billions of years ago may not hold up, according to new computer simulations that counter decades of scientific thinking. The finding suggests the fragile organic molecules supposedly carried by the icy objects would have been destroyed on impact, upending an established origin of life theory that dates back to at least 1961 [with earlier versions postulated in 1908]... Early in its history — over 4 billion years ago — Earth may have experienced a period of heavy bombardment from more than 100,000 comets larger than 100 meters (328 feet), according to the new study, published Wednesday in the journal Scientific Reports. Those impacts, however, were mostly too heavy for life-starting molecules to withstand. The team used the latest models of comet formation and evolution to simulate this early planetary period 100,000 times. "Given what we know about surface environments on the early Earth, on average, our simulations found that there were no successful impacts," said lead study author Richard Anslow, who conducted the research while completing his doctorate at the Institute of Astronomy of the University of Cambridge in the United Kingdom... "The typical velocities of these comets when they impact the Earth meant that actually very few, if any, would have been able to deliver intact organic molecules, so comets actually don't seem to be as useful for prebiotic chemistry as was previously thought," Anslow said. More precisely, 54% of the simulations showed no impact at all, while the remaining 46% had at least one and a "tiny minority" returned up to three collisions, Anslow said. "We can't rule out confidently that there was never a successful impact — there could have been one of these fluke impacts." However, such flukes had to occur in a "perfect location" that already met several important conditions, including the presence of liquid water and other chemicals needed to suppor
articles.summary: 新计算机模拟显示，彗星携带的脆弱有机分子难以在撞击中存活，生命基石或非由史前彗星送达地球。

articles.title: Recycling ANSI Art: Tracing the Origins of BBS Logon Screens
articles.content: BBS-era "door" games are preserved by the site Break Into Chat, along with their history. Now the site's actually traced the origins of several ANSI art screens in the 1980s and "how different people later transformed the original images," starting from one of the most popular bulletin board systems in St. Louis, Missouri. Slashdot reader Kirkman14 writes: "Fire Escape" was curator of the authoritative list of bulletin board systems in St. Louis's area code and sysop of the area's most popular board. Like many sysops of that time, Fire Escape enlivened her bulletin board by finding and repurposing older ANSI art. Eventually her BBS had 18 different logon screens in its rotation, many of which featured flames or mushroom clouds or made liberal use of red and yellow. Break Into Chat follows the trail: Some, maybe even most, of Fire Escape's logon screens had actually been adapted from old school "public domain" ANSI art drawn in the late 1980s and early 1990s by folks such as Michael C. Ling, Lora Ruffner (aka "Ebony Eyes") and Violet Stymacks.... Stymacks was unusually generous with her ANSI art. When she first began drawing, she combed through Fidonet node lists looking for bulletin boards with interesting or inspiring names. When she found one, she would draw an ANSI screen that fit the board's theme, then send it to the sysop. Eventually, sysops began seeking her out, too. By late 1990, she claimed that 500 bulletin boards were using her screens. Three years later, that total had tripled, according to Boardwatch . I believe it — I have located more than 1,100 of her pieces so far. She was so prolific that it would be surprising if she hadn't reused or remixed her own work over the years... [D]id they intend for other people to do so? Or would they have considered such borrowing or adapting as "ripping" or just plain "stealing"? These questions have dogged the BBS, ASCII art, and ANSI art scenes from the beginning. A freelance writer named Patrick Grote grappled wi
articles.summary: Break Into Chat 网站追溯1980年代 BBS 登录界面 ANSI 艺术图的来源，并记录后人如何改造这些原始图像。

articles.title: French Lawmakers Back Per-Gigabyte Internet Traffic Tax
articles.content: Companies like Google, Netflix, TikTok, and Meta may soon owe the French government, reports Tom's Hardware: France has approved a proposed tax that aims to tax the amount of internet data per gigabyte sent to French users in the country... According to minutes released by the National Assembly, members voted 11-10 in support of the motion on October 30 — which now means the new law has been added to the country's next budget, despite major opposition from the government side and the finance committee rapporteur. The latest amendment, introduced by socialist lawmaker Laurent Lhardit, could see content providers pay €0.055 (roughly $0.06) to the government for every gigabyte of content distributed to French users. With approximately 154 million users and counting in France, the proposal's authors say such a tax could generate around €10 billion ($11.2 billion) in annual revenue for the government. The said proposal, though yet to be passed as it must survive further parliamentary scrutiny, aims at companies that generate substantial internet traffic as opposed to taxing their advertising revenue, profits and subscriptions. Its explanatory notes particularly mention Google, Meta, Netflix, Amazon, and content delivery network Akamai as major potential contributors. Notably, TikTok and other similar platforms could fall under this broader scope depending on how these rules are applied. Internet service providers, including Orange Free and Liad, would be required to measure the volume of data and identify the companies responsible for sending it to French users. The Data will then be collected and submitted quarterly to France's tax administration under the supervision of telecommunications watchdog Arcep. The measure becomes law if it clears the remaining stages of France's budget process, the article points out, "with parliament scheduled to vote on the budget's first section in early November." "VideoLAN, the French nonprofit organization behind the VLC media player,
articles.summary: 法国国民议会通过按每GB流量向谷歌、Netflix、TikTok、Meta 等公司征税的提案，后续将进入正式立法程序。

articles.title: NASA Seeks Proposals for Reboosting the Hubble Space Telescope
articles.content: The Hubble Space Telescope "will plunge back into the atmosphere in the early-to-mid-2030s," reports Ars Technica. So now NASA has released a Request For Information (RFI) "asking commercial companies for ideas on how to reboost, service, or a controlled disposal of Hubble." Specifically, NASA is looking for information about companies' current and near-term capabilities for capturing Hubble and boosting it to an altitude of at least 373 miles (600 km), enhancing the telescope's performance, or guiding Hubble to a controlled reentry. "The requirement includes that the boost and/or servicing mission must not harm the HST and that this mission is expected to occur by 2032," NASA wrote in the RFI. The contractor would be responsible for providing the launch vehicle, servicing spacecraft, mission operations, and "crew if applicable." NASA is not committing to buying a Hubble rescue mission, but officials want to know who might be interested in mounting such a mission, how much it would cost, and which companies would have a realistic shot at reaching Hubble before it falls out of orbit and burns up on reentry. Orbital dynamicists currently predict that it will likely happen in 2033 or 2034 without intervention, but reentry forecasts can change based on solar activity... A reboost to NASA's requirement of 373 miles (600 km) would likely keep Hubble in orbit for at least 25 more years. "NASA last raised the orbit of Hubble in 2002," the article points out, "when the Space Shuttle Columbia visited the observatory for a servicing mission." The final shuttle servicing flight in 2009 did not reboost the telescope's orbit, and with the retirement of the shuttle fleet two years later, Hubble has steadily lost altitude with no way to stave off eventual destruction... NASA's newer flagship observatories, sometimes described as successors to Hubble, are not actually one-for-one replacements. Hubble is tuned to observe the Universe in visible and ultraviolet light, while the Webb a
articles.summary: 哈勃望远镜预计2030年代初中期再入大气层，NASA 发布信息征询，寻求商业公司提供抬轨、维修或受控处置方案。

articles.title: Dozens of Unexplained Drones Have Buzzed America's Nuclear Plants Since 2024
articles.content: Slashdot reader ElectricVs shares this report from American Buildout, a new site covering "the intersection of data centers, energy and power, finance, and Main Street." Dozens of unexplained drones flew over and near U.S. nuclear facilities between February 2024 and March 2026, according to records the Nuclear Regulatory Commission made public this week. In all, facility operators filed 67 reports of drones over or near 28 sites in 17 states. They include the Three Mile Island site near Middletown, Pennsylvania., where Constellation Energy plans to restart Unit 1 as the Crane Clean Energy Center. In one incident, about five drones flew roughly 100 feet above the [970-megawatt] reactor building at River Bend Station in Louisiana. The story was first reported by the publication The Liberation Times. The NRC published the documents on its website in response to the publication's freedom of information request... Every entry carries the status "Closed Unresolved." "Most of the incidents happened after dark," the article points out, "and none of the records identifies a drone operator. About half of the incidents, 33 of 67, occurred in an eight-week window between Dec. 3, 2024, and Jan. 24, 2025." (Virginia's Surry Power Station experienced five different incidents in December of 2024, including one involving "at least eight drones in two waves.") 100 miles west of Chicago, "drone activity" continued for more than two hours at the Byron Nuclear Station, where two separate drones were reported. In Waterford, Connecticut, "security observed four drones flying back and forth..." The article notes a 2024 paper from the Nuclear Regulatory Commission citing a 2019 analysis that "concluded U.S. plants had no risk-significant vulnerabilities that adversaries could exploit with commercially available drones to cause radiological sabotage, or theft or diversion of special nuclear material." Read more of this story at Slashdot.
articles.summary: 记录显示2024年2月至2026年3月间，数十架不明无人机飞越美国核设施附近，引发安全担忧。

articles.title: Flock Reinstalled Its Cameras After Another City Canceled Its Contract
articles.content: Earlier The Drive reported a police chief "had to direct his staff to disconnect the power cords from Flock cameras in Plymouth, Minnesota after Flock Safety ignored and failed to respond to the department's notice the city was canceling its service. "But in other instances Flock's gone and reinstalled cameras without permission," The Drive reported this week: On September 29th the city of Dayton, Minnesota posted a community update on its Facebook page alerting residents that Flock had installed and put into service two cameras against the City's direction without authorization... "The City notified Flock on September 18, 2026, that the program was on hold, and no work orders were to be completed. Unfortunately, the City's direction was not followed, and the camera was placed back into service without authorization." The statement continued and noted, "Following the report, City staff reviewed locations throughout the community to determine whether any additional cameras had been reinstalled, and one additional location was identified. The Police Department has been notified, and both cameras will be removed promptly...." The Minnesota cities of both St. Paul and Crystal told Kare 11 that they removed the Flock cameras themselves following their respective city council votes in August and September respectively. The cameras are stored and are still waiting to be picked up by Flock. Crystal Chief of Police Pete Underthun told Kare 11, "Once we made this decision, I personally went to the locations and removed the cameras and poles myself." Chief Underthun noted, "We are still working with the company to close out our contract and for them to pick the cameras up from our garage." Read more of this story at Slashdot.
